output.report_thesis: The evidence presents a decision picture spanning observed and anticipated search pressure, stated newsroom content priorities and creator concerns, and prospective platform/AI revenue alongside assessments of current newsroom AI initiatives.

themes.theme: Search signals differ in status: aggregate Chartbeat data show Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025, while the average slider score among 268 Q5 respondents indicates an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years, not an observed change.

Among 264 Q13 respondents, reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are perceptions of importance, not newsroom behavior.
Among 263 Q19 respondents, 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among 265 Q11 respondents, the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far was “promising” for 44%, “limited” for 42%, “transformational” for 13%, and “disappointing” for 2%.

Publisher respondents (base 272) express varied expectations for possible AI-company licensing deals around news-content IP in about three years: 69% expect at least some income, comprising 49% expecting a minor source and 20% a significant source; 20% expect no income, 11% do not know, and 0% expect a main source.

Among respondents from commercial publishers excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% expect funding from platforms, including AI platforms, to be likely important or very important for their company in 2026; the chart annotates this as up 17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.
